facts.statement: The genus Quinkana was described by Molnar in 1981.
facts.quote: authority: Molnar, 1981

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Quinkana is Quinkana fortirostrum.
facts.quote: type_species: Quinkana fortirostrum

facts.statement: Four species are currently recognized within the genus Quinkana: Q. fortirostrum, Q. timara, Q. babarra, and Q. meboldi.
facts.quote: subdivision: * Quinkana fortirostrum Molnar, 1981 (type) Quinkana timara Megirian, 1994 Quinkana babarra Willis & Mackness, 1996 Quinkana meboldi Willis, 1997

facts.statement: Quinkana lived in Australia from approximately 25 million years ago until about 20,000 years ago.
facts.quote: Quinkana is an extinct genus of mekosuchine crocodylians that lived in Australia from about 25 million to about 20,000 years ago

facts.statement: The majority of Quinkana fossils have been found in Queensland.
facts.quote: with the majority of fossils having been found in Queensland

facts.statement: Quinkana is characterized by ziphodont teeth that were recurved, serrated, and blade-like.
facts.quote: Quinkana is primarily known for its ziphodont teeth, meaning they were recurved, serrated and possessed flattened sides that gave them a blade-like shape

facts.statement: Quinkana is distinguished by a combination of ziphodont teeth and a deep, altirostral skull.
facts.quote: The genus is distinguishable by the combination of these ziphodont teeth and a deep, altirostral skull

facts.statement: Quinkana is typically estimated to be about 3 meters long and weigh around 200 kilograms.
facts.quote: Quinkana is typically estimated to be around 3 m in length and to weigh around 200 kg

facts.statement: Paleontologists debate whether Quinkana was terrestrial or semi-aquatic.
facts.quote: The genus has been argued amongst paleontologists to be either terrestrial or semi-aquatic, with both sides providing a variety of arguments

facts.statement: The ecological role of Quinkana in Late Pleistocene Australia is debated.
facts.quote: The role Quinkana filled in the ecosystems of Late Pleistocene Australia has also been a matter of debate

facts.statement: Charles Walter De Vis found early Quinkana fossils in the Darling Downs region of Queensland in 1886.
facts.quote: Some of the earliest fossil finds now attributed to this genus date as far back as 1886, when Charles Walter De Vis found a variety of fossil bones, including those of Quinkana, in the Darling Downs region of Queensland

facts.statement: Lyndsey Hawkins discovered significant Quinkana fossil material in the Tea Tree Cave in 1970.
facts.quote: The research history of Quinkana began in earnest in 1970 with the discovery of fossil material in the Tea Tree Cave (part of the Chillagoe caves of Northern Queensland) by Lyndsey Hawkins

facts.statement: Michael Archer recovered a second ziphodont crocodilian from the Texas Caves in 1975.
facts.quote: Additional discoveries were made in the years following this event, with a second ziphodont crocodilian being recovered from the Texas Caves in southern Queensland in 1975 by Michael Archer

facts.statement: The Texas Cave crocodile specimen was described in 1977 by Max Hecht and Michael Archer.
facts.quote: The Texas Cave crocodile, as it was referred to in later publications, consisted of a partial maxilla with some additional bone fragments that would be described in 1977 by Max Hecht and Michael Archer

facts.statement: Quinkana survived the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene arid period but went extinct at the end of the Pleistocene.
facts.quote: Though successfully surviving a drastic arid period that marked the transition from the Late Miocene to the Early Pliocene, Quinkana would eventually die out towards the end of the Pleistocene

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that intense aridification caused Quinkana's extinction by drying river basins and destroying forests.
facts.quote: The precise reasons for Quinkana's disappearance are unknown, but it is hypothesized that another period of intense aridification gradually dried up the river basins and destroyed the forests that the crocodilian inhabited

facts.statement: Paleontologist Ralph Molnar described the genus Quinkana in 1981 based mainly on a rostrum found in the Chillagoe caves.
facts.quote: Ralph Molnar, who described Quinkana as a genus in 1981 based primarily on the rostrum from the Chillagoe caves

facts.statement: Molnar tentatively assigned the Texas Cave crocodile to the genus Quinkana but hesitated to identify it as a specific species due to slight differences that might be due to growth stages.
facts.quote: Molnar also assigned the Texas Cave crocodile to the genus but was hesitant to make an identification on a species level given some slight differences that may or may not be the result of ontogeny

facts.statement: In 1993, various Australasian fossil crocodilian species, including those of Quinkana, were placed in the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: various species being described and finally being placed in the subfamily Mekosuchinae in 1993

facts.statement: Paleontologist Dirk Megirian named the second species, Quinkana timara, in 1994.
facts.quote: in 1994, Quinkana timara was named by paleontologist Dirk Megirian as a second species within the genus

facts.statement: The holotype of Quinkana timara consists of snout fragments found in limestone at the Bullock Creek Locality in the Northern Territory.
facts.quote: The holotype of Q. timara (NTM P895-19) consists of various snout fragments discovered within limestone found in the Bullock Creek Locality in the Northern Territory

facts.statement: The holotype of Quinkana babarra, a maxilla fragment, was uncovered in 1991 at the Dick's Mother Lode Quarry in northeast Queensland.
facts.quote: The holotype (QM F23220), a fragment of the maxilla, was uncovered in 1991 by Mackness at the Dick's Mother Lode Quarry in the Charters Towers Region of northeast Queensland

facts.statement: A notable later find was a ziphodont tooth of Quinkana discovered in the Late Pleistocene King Creek catchment of the eastern Darling Downs.
facts.quote: Among the more notable later finds was the discovery of a ziphodont tooth in the Late Pleistocene King Creek catchment of the eastern Darling Downs

facts.statement: The type species Quinkana fortirostrum was described in 1981 by Ralph Molnar from a partial skull found in middle Pleistocene cave deposits in Queensland.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus, Q. fortirostrum was described in 1981 by Ralph Molnar based on a partial skull collected from middle Pleistocene cave deposits in Queensland

facts.statement: Although the genus is known for ziphodont teeth, the holotype of Q. fortirostrum did not preserve teeth in their sockets, so this feature is inferred.
facts.quote: While the genus as a whole is best known for its ziphodont teeth, they are only inferred for the holotype, as the actual fossil did not preserve with any teeth still in their sockets

facts.statement: The name Q. fortirostrum means "strong beak," referring to the species' snout.
facts.quote: The species name was based on the Latin words "fortis" and "rostrum" meaning "strong" and "beak" (in reference to the species' snout) respectively

facts.statement: Quinkana timara is known from more material than other species, including a partial snout and the antorbital region.
facts.quote: Q. timara is known from a lot more material than the other species, with the type material consisting of a partial snout and the antorbital region of what was likely the same specimen

facts.statement: Quinkana timara is defined by having a narrower snout and a proportionally larger antorbital shelf compared to Q. fortirostrum.
facts.quote: The species was defined as having a "narrower snout" and "proportionally larger antorbital shelf [opening in the skull]" than Q. fortirostrum

facts.statement: Quinkana timara lived during the middle to late Miocene in the Northern Territory of Australia.
facts.quote: Q. timara is known from the Bullock Creek Locality near Camfield Station in Australia's Northern Territory, dating to the middle to late Miocene

facts.statement: Ralph Molnar cautiously proposed that Quinkana was a terrestrial predator based on its cranial anatomy, though he acknowledged counterarguments to this idea.
facts.quote: Based on its unique cranial anatomy, Molnar cautiously proposed that Quinkana could have been a terrestrial predator, though he himself acknowledged several counterarguments to this hypothesis

facts.statement: There is ongoing debate regarding Quinkana's role in prehistoric Australian ecosystems and whether it was terrestrial.
facts.quote: During this period the ecology and habits of Quinkana gained more attention, with repeated debate on its role in Australia's prehistoric ecosystems and whether or not it was terrestrial

facts.statement: The generic name Quinkana is derived from the Quinkans, spirits of the Gugu-Yalanji people of Northern Queensland.
facts.quote: Etymology Its generic name was derived from the Quinkans, a type of spirit of the Northern Queensland aboriginal Gugu-Yalanji people

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra was named in 1996 and is known from the early Pliocene Allingham Formation of Queensland.
facts.quote: Named in 1996, this species is known from the early Pliocene Allingham Formation of Queensland but only preserved through a fragment of the maxilla and a few isolated teeth.

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra likely had a wider and shorter snout compared to Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara.
facts.quote: Q. babarra can be differentiated from Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara by likely having a wider and shorter snout.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi was found at the White Hunter Site in Riversleigh, northwestern Queensland, and dates to approximately 25 million years ago.
facts.quote: This species was found at the White Hunter Site in Riversleigh, northwestern Queensland which is a late Oligocene deposit (ca. 25 Ma), making it the oldest species of Quinkana described.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi is generally regarded as one of the smaller species of Quinkana.
facts.quote: It is generally regarded as being among the smaller species of Quinkana.

facts.statement: A late Pleistocene tooth found in 2013 at the Kings Creek site in southeastern Queensland resembles teeth of Quinkana fortirostrum, despite the species' holotype being toothless.
facts.quote: A late Pleistocene tooth (QM F57032) was found in 2013 in the Kings Creek site of southeastern Queensland and shares similarities with teeth traditionally assigned to Quinkana fortirostrum, though the holotype of said species is actually toothless.

facts.statement: It is debated whether a metatarsal bone found in 1992 at the Bluff Downs fossil site belongs to Quinkana babarra or a different crocodilian.
facts.quote: A metatarsal bone (QM F30566) was found in 1992 in the Bluff Downs fossil site near Allingham in northern Queensland. This specimen could represent a rare limb element, but it is just as possible that it belonged to a different type of crocodilian altogether.

facts.statement: The proportions of the snout and specialized dentition of Quinkana are often cited as evidence for a terrestrial lifestyle.
facts.quote: Quinkana is best distinguished from other mekosuchines by the proportions of its snout and its highly specialised dentition, both of which are oftentimes cited as evidence for a more terrestrial lifestyle.

facts.statement: The snout of Quinkana fortirostrum is deep and angular, resembling proportions found in Paleogene planocraniids and Cretaceous to Miocene sebecosuchians.
facts.quote: The snout of Q. fortirostrum is noticeably deep and angular, its proportions somewhat resembling much older fossil crocodylomorphs such as the planocraniids that existed during the Paleogene across the Northern Hemisphere and the sebecosuchians that were primarily found in South America from the Cretaceous to the Miocene.

facts.statement: Molnar describes the skull of Quinkana fortirostrum as broader than planocraniids and sebecosuchians, yet deeper than any modern crocodilian.
facts.quote: Molnar describes the skull of Q. fortirostrum as being broader than that of members of the aforementioned groups, yet also distinctly deeper (higher) than those of any modern crocodilians with a distinct trapezoid cross-section.

facts.statement: Quinkana timara, an older Miocene form, had slender jaws that resemble those of Boverisuchus in proportions.
facts.quote: Q. timara, an older form from the Miocene, had noticeably more slender jaws that most closely resemble those of Boverisuchus in proportions.

facts.statement: Ristevski and colleagues argue that many isolated teeth traditionally assigned to Quinkana may actually belong to other distinct ziphodont crocodilian genera.
facts.quote: Given the large quantity of ziphodont crocodilians likely to be distinct from Quinkana, Ristevski and colleagues have argued that many isolated teeth traditionally referred to the Quinkana could also belong to these other forms.

facts.statement: The narial rim surrounding the nostrils was weakly developed in Q. timara but very prominent in Q. fortirostrum.
facts.quote: The nares are further surrounded by a ring of bone, referred to as the narial rim, that is only weakly developed in Q. timara and very prominent in Q. fortirostrum.

facts.statement: Steep maxillae gave Quinkana skulls a deep, altirostral appearance.
facts.quote: The maxillae are steep, which gives the skull of Quinkana its altirostral (deep) appearance.

facts.statement: The maxillae of Quinkana inclined at a 60° angle at the front and 45° at the back as the skull widened.
facts.quote: Towards the front they incline at a 60° angle, whereas further towards the back the skull becomes wider and the maxillae only incline at an angle of 45°.

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone shape indicates Quinkana had eyes facing sideways, a trait of terrestrial crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: The shape of the lacrimal further indicates that Quinkana had eyes that faced sideways rather than up, a hallmark of more terrestrial crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Megirian refuted Molnar's claim that the jugal bone did not extend in front of the eye orbits in Quinkana.
facts.quote: Initially, Molnar described the jugal bone as not extending in front of the orbits, a claim later refuted by Megirian.

facts.statement: The jugal bone extends in front of the eyes in both Q. timara and the Texas Caves cranium assigned to Quinkana.
facts.quote: Not only does the jugal extend in front of the eyes in Q. timara, but it also does in the Texas Caves cranium assigned to the genus by Molnar.

facts.statement: The ventral side of the jugal bone in Quinkana had a sculptured area similar to that of the American alligator.
facts.quote: the lower (ventral) side of the jugal was covered in a distinct sculptured area similar to that seen in today's American alligator.

facts.statement: The vertical orientation of the postorbital bar suggests the skull table overhung the temporal region in Quinkana.
facts.quote: This would suggest that the skull table would somewhat overhang the temporal region.

facts.statement: Q. fortirostrum had a rounded crest extending along both the maxilla and premaxilla, while Q. timara had a crest restricted to the maxilla.
facts.quote: The skull of Q. fortirostrum has a rounded crest which extends along both bones, whereas in Q. timara the crest was restricted entirely to the former.

facts.statement: Q. babarra lacked a full crest and instead had multiple isolated peaks, with the largest matching the crest tip of Q. fortirostrum.
facts.quote: Q. babarra meanwhile was noted to not have had a full crest but rather multiple isolated peaks, the largest of which corresponding to the end of the crest in Q. fortirostrum.

facts.statement: Distinct knobs on the lacrimal and prefrontal bones were found in older Quinkana species, though less pronounced than in the Pleistocene Q. fortirostrum.
facts.quote: These features are not exclusive to Quinkana fortirostrum, but can also be observed in the older species, if not as pronounced as in the Pleistocene form.

facts.statement: Megirian hypothesizes that the development of skull knobs in Quinkana may be related to age.
facts.quote: Megirian hypothesizes that age could be a factor in this, with the features changing as the individual grows older.

facts.statement: The bottom of the Quinkana maxilla lacked the wave-like festooning pattern seen in many other crocodilians.
facts.quote: The bottom of the maxilla is slightly convex and does not display the same pattern of wave-like rises and drops (known as festooning) that is seen in many other crocodilians.

facts.statement: Q. fortirostrum had a nearly straight toothrow due to a lack of vertical festooning, while Q. timara showed slightly more developed festooning.
facts.quote: The lack of vertical festooning is especially prominent in Q. fortirostrum, in which the toothrow is nearly straight, though slightly more developed in the older Q. timara.

facts.statement: Quinkana skulls viewed from above lacked the sinuous outline of other crocodilians because lateral festooning was poorly developed.
facts.quote: Lateral festooning was likewise not well developed, which means that when viewed from above skulls of Quinkana did not have the sinuous outline like other crocodilians, which is marked by the presence of multiple constrictions and expansions of the maxillae.

facts.statement: Even in Q. babarra and Q. meboldi, the most prominent festooning in Quinkana was barely present.
facts.quote: The most prominent festooning in Quinkana is expressed in Q. babarra and Q. meboldi, however even in these species the condition is barely present.

facts.statement: The ventral view of the Quinkana skull shows a U-shaped contact between the premaxilla and maxilla and an incisive foramen that is wider than it is long.
facts.quote: the ventral contact between premaxilla and maxilla is U-shape and the incisive foramen is wider than it is long

facts.statement: In Q. fortirostrum, the palatine bones end between the palatal fenestrae and contact the maxilla via a V-shaped suture.
facts.quote: the palatines in Q. fortirostrum seem to end between the fenestrae where they contact the maxilla via a V-shaped suture

facts.statement: In Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara, the medial location of lower jaw reception pits relative to upper teeth indicates the animal had an overbite.
facts.quote: In Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara, reception pits for the teeth of the lower jaw are located medially relative to the teeth of the premaxilla and maxilla, indicating that this animal had an overbite

facts.statement: Among several mekosuchines with laterally flattened teeth, only Quinkana is considered to have truly ziphodont teeth.
facts.quote: only those of Quinkana are considered to be truly ziphodont

facts.statement: In Q. fortirostrum, the oblique orientation of the teeth is best observed ventrolaterally.
facts.quote: In Quinkana fortirostrum for example this orientation is best observed ventrolaterally

facts.statement: Unlike Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara, the teeth in Q. babarra align with each other rather than having an oblique orientation.
facts.quote: unlike in Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara with their oblique tooth orientation, the axis of the teeth in Q. babarra fall in line with each other
